quote: Yes, I know! I was shocked too. But it seems that after scientists measured the forces exerted on the cup by each of your fingers, your thumb, and your palm, they found there was no force left over—so the force exerted by your hand must be zero.
content: The parody has a target, Kim’s causal exclusion argument (Mind in a Physical World, 1998), and the parody is the standard objection to it, made in the literature with examples of exactly this shape (Yablo (1992) on determinables and determinates; Bennett (2003)). But the joke works by switching the subject. Kim’s argument is about properties, not objects: nobody thinks the hand is an entity additional to its parts, and the exclusion question is whether the hand’s grip, a functional property realized by many configurations of fingers, does any causal work over and above the microphysical properties that realize it on this occasion. On that question the parody is silent, and the sequence’s own thesis, that higher-level descriptions are “in the map,” is the exclusion thesis about properties restated. So the essay ridicules a position with an object-level example and then adopts the property-level version of the same position on the next page. Whether composition is identity is itself contested (Lewis, Baxter; van Inwagen’s Material Beings, 1990, holds that there are no hands, only simples arranged handwise, and takes the view seriously enough to write a book), and the essay’s “physical identity” between hand and parts is an answer to that dispute, not a datum.

quote: All of these are cases of Mind Projection Fallacy, and what I call “naive philosophical realism”—the confusion of philosophical intuitions for direct, veridical information about reality. Your inability to imagine something is just a computational fact about what your brain can or can’t imagine. Another brain might work differently.
content: The distinction the essay is drawing, between what one can conceive and what is possible, is the subject of Chalmers’s “Does Conceivability Entail Possibility?” (2002, in Gendler and Hawthorne, Conceivability and Possibility, a book with no DOI), which separates prima facie from ideal conceivability and primary from secondary possibility, and states the zombie argument in terms of ideal conceivability precisely to meet the objection that a mere failure to notice a contradiction proves nothing. The essay presents the distinction as its own correction to philosophers who have not noticed it; the philosopher it will spend the next three essays attacking built his argument on it. As for the rule that intuitions are not evidence about reality, the sequence itself does not follow it: Zombies! Zombies? ends by advising the reader that “on a core gut level, this just doesn’t look like the way reality could really really work,” and Dissolving the Question makes a feeling of resolution the criterion of success. Intuitions are evidence of something in both cases; the essay allows them when they point its way.

quote: It is conceptually possible to you that 235,757 is prime, because you don’t know any better. But it isn’t logically possible that 235,757 is prime; if you were logically omniscient, 235,757 would be obviously composite (and you would know the factors).
content: The number is composite: 235,757 = 431 × 547. The example is sound, and the notion of impossible possible worlds that it motivates (Hintikka, “Impossible Possible Worlds Vindicated,” Journal of Philosophical Logic, 1975, whose paper coined the phrase; Rantala’s urn models) is the right tool for probability over logical uncertainty. The annotation is here to note that the same tool cuts against the sequence’s use of “logically possible” in the zombie essays. If logical possibility is fixed by what an omniscient reasoner would find, then whether the Zombie World is logically possible is a question no one can currently answer, and the essay’s later confidence that it is impossible is a conceptual-possibility judgment of the kind this paragraph warns against, made by a brain that, like the reader’s about 235,757, does not know any better. The distinction is symmetrical; the sequence applies it in one direction.
